newsitem.title: POLAND: NO ROOM FOR SLOWER ZLOTY DEVALUATION-POLISH FINMIN.
newsitem.headline: NO ROOM FOR SLOWER ZLOTY DEVALUATION-POLISH FINMIN.

text.p: The current state of Poland's economy does not permit a reduction in the monthly rate of the crawling peg devaluation of the zloty against a basket of currencies, Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday.

"We are in a situation where we certainly should not reduce the crawling devaluation of the zloty and we are not taking any such decisions," Belka told a meeting of executives representing Poland's largest 500 companies.

The zloty is currently devalued at a monthly rate of one percent against a basket of five western currencies which translates in the annual rate of 12.7 percent but the 1997 budget assumes a slower annual devaluation of 9.1 percent.

Several business groups and economists have however said widening trade and current account deficits signalled the zloty was too strong after its strong real appreciation in 1995 and early in 1996 and its rise should be capped or reversed.
Belka told the meeting he saw curbing the trade deficit as the biggest challenge of Poland's economy this year but stressed there was no need for radical shifts in policy.

"The trade deficit is the biggest problem of Poland's economy, bigger than inflation...but as long as exports grow and investment goods dominate imports concerns related to the current account deficit are muted. Right now we do not face a need of a dramatic change in economic policy," Belka said.
Last year Poland's current account merchandise trade deficit widened to $8.15 billion from $2.10 billion in 1995.
